new_statements.quote: The occurrence of the tone is the most characteristic feature in this dialect. It is not possible to isolate stress from tone. Both are mixed together. But stress is not phonemic as it does not show any contrast in meaning. Only tone is recognized as phonemic. It is significant to observe that each phonologic word has only one lexically significant and contrastive tone. ... In disyllabic words mostly the tone occurs on the initial syllable but it occurs on the second syllable in the following positions: I Tone occurs on the causal suffix /-a/ If the first syllable has central vowel and the second peripheral vowel and the intervening consonant is single, then, the second syllable carries the tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kandiali is a three-tone (low/mid/high) Panjabi-type system; stress co-occurs with the single tonic syllable of the phonological word and is not contrastive by itself. The tonic syllable is by default the first; it is the second when the first syllable has a short/central vowel (I, ə, U) and the second a long/peripheral vowel with only a single consonant between them (typically causatives), or when the word begins with a prefix (kə-rup, bə-cɛn); in tri-/quadrisyllables with central V1 and peripheral later vowels the tone is on the 2nd syllable, except that a following cluster/geminate keeps it on the 1st (bUDDiã, muttərna). In compounds the first member carries the tone; postpositions, conjunctions and particles are atonic 'with zero stress'. I.e. weight-conditioned tonic-syllable placement within an initial two-syllable window.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; non-tonic elements of compounds and clitics are 'atonic', with tone and pitch spreading over them.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone stays on the first syllable when a consonant sequence/geminate follows the central vowel (/bUDDiã/ 'old f.pl.', /muttərna/ 'to urinate'); prefixed words take tone on the 2nd syllable; compounds on the first element; postpositions/particles atonic.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'phonologic word' (one contrastive tone per phonological word); intonation (pitch levels 1-4, terminals) treated separately in 1.4.2.4. Statement is for Kandiali of Shahpur Kandi (NE Gurdaspur), not for Standard Chambeali of Chamba town.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is for KANDIALI (/kaNDyaLi/), the speech of the Kandi tract in the NE hills of (former) Gurdaspur district, Punjab (Shahpur Kandi / Dhar area, now Pathankot district), bordering Chamba's Bhattiyat, Kathua (J&K) and Kangra. It has no glottocode of its own; Glottolog files Tripathi 1975 as the sole descriptive reference under cham1307 Chambeali, but Grierson (LSI IX.1 p. 637) treated Kandiali as a Dogri [dogr1250] / Panjabi mixture, and Tripathi himself calls it a Western Pahari dialect 'merging into Panjabi' that 'closely resembles Chambeali and Kangri [kang1280]'; geographically it is nearest to Bhattiyali [bhat1263]. It is a fully tonal Panjabi-type variety. Standard Chambeali of Chamba town (the cham1307 reference variety, described by Bailey 1908, Grierson 1916 and Baskaran 2023 in LSI-Himachal Pradesh) has NO published stress statement in any source opened: LSI-HP 2023 lists only length and nasalisation as suprasegmentals. A catalog entry should be labelled 'Kandiali (Tripathi 1975), filed under cham1307 by Glottolog' rather than 'Chambeali'.
